newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Arafat urges bigger Mideast role for Russia.
newsitem.headline: Arafat urges bigger Mideast role for Russia.

text.p: Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat on Wednesday praised Russia's contribution to the Middle East peace process but his warm words could not conceal Moscow's reduced influence in the region.

"Russia, as a co-sponsor of the peace process (with the United States), plays an important role in the Middle East," Arafat told a joint news conference with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov at the end of a two-day visit to Moscow.
"We have agreed in our talks that Russia should step up its involvement in the peace process."

Arafat, who held talks with President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday, said Moscow would be the venue for the next meeting of a multilateral cooperation group on the regional peace process, which includes the U.S., Russia and the European Union.
Interfax news agency, quoting a Foreign Ministry source, said the meeting would take place in late March and would also include several Middle East countries.

"Our line on resolving the situation in the Middle East and strengthening friendship with the Arab world is not only traditional but also strategic," said Primakov, an Arab speaker with long experience of regional issues.

Russia, dogged by severe economic problems, has lost much of its clout in the Middle East since Soviet times when its strong support for Palestinian self-rule helped counter Washington's pro-Israel stance.

Primakov has tried to reassert Russia's regional influence since becoming foreign minister in January 1996 but Moscow played no part in last month's U.S.-brokered peace deal under which Israel agreed to hand over 80 percent of the town of Hebron to the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
Asked about Russia's reduced role, Primakov said jokingly: "Not everything depends on economic power. Maybe we shall use other means (of exerting influence)".
"I hope that in a few years Russia will have greater opportunities to develop economic cooperation with the Palestinian state," he said.
Primakov said Russia would continue to provide economic aid to the Palestinian Authority within its limited means, including money for the training of Palestinian policemen.
He also backed Arafat's call for a lifting of Israel's blockade of Palestinian territory, imposed following Moslem suicide bombings last year.
Arafat said the blockade cost his people six to eight million dollars daily and added that aid from foreign donors covered barely half the losses incurred.

"Those who come to power must uphold the documents signed by their predecessors," said Primakov, referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hardline stance on the Palestinian question since replacing Shimon Peres last year.
Arafat also urged Russia, the United States and the European Union to dissuade Israel from resettling Jews on the West Bank, saying this contravened the peace agreement signed in Madrid in 1993.
Netanyahu is expected to visit Moscow next month.

Primakov said it was important that Israelis and Palestinians begin talks on the final status of Jerusalem. The Palestinians want to recover the eastern part of the Holy City and have suggested a joint municipal authority.
Arafat said he had invited Yeltsin to attend celebrations in Bethlehem in the year 2000 to mark the anniversary of Christianity, and that Yeltsin had happily accepted.
Arafat also held talks on Wednesday with Patriarch Alexei, head of Russia's Orthodox Church.
